```{r setup}
#| include: false
if (nzchar(params$pkg_path) && dir.exists(file.path(params$pkg_path, "R"))) {
  devtools::load_all(params$pkg_path, quiet = TRUE)
} else {
  library(stateELP)
}

spec <- read_el_spec(params$spec_file)

# Dev mode by default: the document runs the stage. `results_file` switches to
# RDS mode, which is how the Decision stage will read what earlier stages
# produced. Analysis logic lives in R/, never here: this file holds the prose,
# the captions, and one call per figure or table.
res <- if (!is.null(params$results_file) && nzchar(params$results_file)) {
  readRDS(params$results_file)
} else {
  bundle <- as_el_data(el_long_sim, roster = el_roster_sim,
                       academic = academic_long_sim, spec = spec)
  run_check4(bundle, spec)
}

# `h` is "has it", `n` is "is it missing": Quarto reads a second `!` inside
# `!expr` as a second YAML tag, so the negation needs its own name.
slots <- c("consistency_curve", "youden_j", "j_optimal", "candidate_region",
           "dependence", "policy_as_whole")
h <- vapply(slots, function(s) !is.null(res[[s]]), TRUE)
n <- !h

have_resolution <- !is.na(res$meta$resolution_note)
have_axis <- h[["youden_j"]] && !is.na(res$meta$axis_note)
have_threshold_note <- h[["j_optimal"]] && !is.na(res$meta$threshold_note)

component <- spec_headline_label(spec)
min_cell <- spec_min_cell(spec)

# Captions are built here, not inline: a colon-space inside an `!expr` value
# is read as a YAML mapping and the render fails. Each mark is described only
# when the figure actually draws it.
marks <- character()
if (h[["j_optimal"]] && !is.na(res$j_optimal$J_CUT[[1]])) {
  marks <- c(marks, "the dashed line marks the J optimum among the cuts shown")
}
if (h[["j_optimal"]] && !is.na(res$j_optimal$THRESHOLD[[1]])) {
  marks <- c(marks, paste(
    "the dotted line marks",
    if (isTRUE(res$j_optimal$RULE_IS_TERM[[1]])) {
      "the exit rule's term on this level"
    } else if (isTRUE(res$j_optimal$RULE_IS_ROUTE[[1]])) {
      "the exit rule's route on this level"
    } else {
      "the current exit rule"
    }))
}
if (h[["j_optimal"]] && !is.na(res$j_optimal$AGREE_CUT[[1]])) {
  marks <- c(marks, "the circle marks raw agreement's highest reportable point")
}
marks_text <- if (length(marks)) {
  paste0(toupper(substring(paste(marks, collapse = "; "), 1, 1)),
         substring(paste(marks, collapse = "; "), 2), ". ")
} else ""

curve_cap <- if (h[["youden_j"]]) {
  sprintf(paste(
    "Decision consistency and Youden's J at every candidate cut on the %s",
    "level, grade %s %s, %d. %sSuppressed cuts are not drawn: a cut is shown",
    "only if neither its own cells nor its difference from a neighbouring",
    "published count --- the cut shown before it, or a band boundary Data",
    "Check 3 reports --- would disclose a group of fewer than %d students."),
    component, res$meta$grade, res$meta$subject, res$meta$year, marks_text,
    min_cell)
} else "Decision consistency and Youden's J"

optimum_cap <- if (h[["j_optimal"]]) {
  sprintf(paste(
    "Where J peaks among the cuts that can be shown, the highest reportable",
    "agreement, and how the current rule scores, grade %s %s, %d. Proficient",
    "is the share of these current ELs at or above the content test's",
    "proficiency cut."),
    res$meta$grade, res$meta$subject, res$meta$year)
} else "The J optimum"

table_cap <- if (h[["youden_j"]]) {
  sprintf(paste(
    "Every candidate cut, grade %s %s, %d. A student counts as at/above when",
    "their %s level is at or above the cut. A dash marks a suppressed cut:",
    "one whose own cells, or whose difference from the cut shown before it",
    "or from a band boundary Data Check 3 reports, would disclose a group of",
    "fewer than %d students."),
    res$meta$grade, res$meta$subject, res$meta$year, component, min_cell)
} else "Every candidate cut"
```

## Looking at

Two statistics, computed at every candidate cut on the `r component` level.
At each cut a current EL is classified *ready to exit* if their level is at
or above it, and that classification is set against whether the same student
reached proficiency on the content test that year.

- **Decision consistency** is the share of students for whom the two
  classifications agree.
- **Youden's J** is sensitivity plus specificity, minus one: how well the cut
  separates students who are proficient on the content test from those who
  are not, with the two error *rates* --- the share of proficient students it
  holds back, and the share of not-proficient students it lets exit ---
  weighted the same, however common each group is.

The Process Overview pairs these with a rank-dependence analysis --- the
Betebenner copula / Kendall's-tau method --- that examines where and how
strongly ELP and content performance move together, including in the tails.
That piece is not built yet; *What is not here* says what is turnkey and
what is not.

## Looking for

**Decision consistency's peak --- with a specific caution.** When English
learners' academic-proficiency rate sits well below 50%, as it typically does,
the peak can be distorted, or fail to appear within a realistic range at all,
because the statistic is pulled toward whichever classification is more
common. Calling every student *not ready* already agrees with the content
test for every student who is not proficient, so agreement climbs as the cut
rises and can keep climbing to the top of the scale.

The arithmetic is short. Raising the cut past a level moves agreement up
when most students at that level are *not* proficient, so --- where the
proficiency rate rises steadily with level --- agreement peaks where the rate
among students at a level crosses one half. It moves J up when students at
that level are proficient *less often than the overall base rate*, so J peaks
where the rate crosses the base rate instead. With a base rate below one
half, the J optimum therefore sits at or below the agreement peak, and in
practice usually well below it. That gap is what the figure shows.

**Youden's J corrects for this** by weighting both error rates equally,
however common each kind of student is --- which is why it, and not raw
consistency, is this stage's optimal-cut statistic.

## Interpreting it

**Prefer J over raw decision consistency** as the primary optimal-cut
statistic, because of the base-rate sensitivity above.

**Treat convergence between Data Checks 3 and 4 as the strongest evidence**,
and any single method's result on its own with more caution. Read the
comparison with one fact in mind. Check 3's two landings --- the first band
where half the students reach the proficiency cut, and the `r component`
*scale score* (a different axis from this stage's levels) at which a fitted
logistic crosses 50% --- both mark where proficiency becomes more likely than
not. That is the point raw agreement aims at, not the point J aims at. With a
base rate below one half they should therefore land at or above the J
optimum, or not appear at all: a gap of that sign is expected, not a
disagreement. The informative comparisons are Check 3's band landing against
this stage's agreement curve, and both against J.

**Read the curve's shape, not only its peak.** A J curve that is flat near
its top means several cuts separate students almost equally well, and the
optimum alone overstates how precisely the data locate a threshold. That is
why this stage's eventual output is a candidate region rather than a single
number.

**Remember Prep 3's error-tolerance question here.** Youden's J treats a
false exit and a false hold as equally costly *as rates*: one in ten
proficient students held back counts the same as one in ten not-proficient
students let go. Per student that is not an even trade --- at a low base rate
J weighs each held-back proficient student far more heavily than each
premature exit, and the note beside the figure says by how much. Stakeholders
answer Prep 3's question per student, so if they weigh the two errors
differently from J, that is a deliberate, documented reason to land the final
threshold above or below the J-optimal point --- a values input the statistic
itself cannot supply, not a departure from the evidence.

## Checkpoint

Confirm the analysis is computing **Youden's J, not raw decision consistency
relabeled**, before relying on it as the primary threshold statistic. This is
a demonstrated gap between the two methods, not a theoretical concern: where
the two curves above peak at different cuts, the J optimum is the one this
stage reports. The package holds a small test fixture whose proficiency rate
is well below one half, where the consistency peak and the J optimum diverge
by construction, and the stage must return the J optimum there.

## What is not here

**The candidate region.** The stage's eventual answer is a region, not a
single number, read across every tested grade and annotated with which
grades and years carry the most and least reliable evidence per Data Check 1.
This pass computes one grade and subject; the region across grades is a
later pass.

**The rank-dependence analysis.** What is turnkey and what is custom:
decision consistency and Youden's J --- the Cook et al. methods --- are built
here and run on any delivery. The copula / Kendall's-tau dependence analysis,
which asks where and how strongly ELP and content performance move together
and whether they couple differently at the low end (expected: independence,
noise) than at the high end (expected: real signal), is custom. It has no
package support yet, and its slot stays empty until it does.

::: {.callout-important appearance="default" icon=false}
## What these curves can and cannot say here

On simulated data the J-optimal point is **machinery, not a finding.** Where
it lands is set by the generator's parameters --- how far EL content scores
sit below the cut, how steeply they rise with ELP level, how much they vary
--- and by how the simulated exit rule thins the top of the level scale. The
figure demonstrates that the curves build, suppress and render correctly, and
that the two statistics part ways at a low base rate as the method says they
should; it is not evidence about where any state's threshold belongs. Run
against a real delivery, the same figure is the stage's substantive output.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="default" icon=false}
## Decide before moving on

1. **A candidate region** --- not necessarily a single number --- supported by
   the balance of evidence across Data Checks 3--4, noting explicitly which
   grades and years carry the most and least reliable evidence per Data
   Check 1's findings.
2. **Record Prep 3's error-tolerance answer beside the region** --- or that
   the question is still open --- as an input to the Decision stage, which
   chooses where in the region to land.
:::
